headline: Halfway Rock holds the pattern: mackerel thick, bass working the ledges on the push
subhead: The Gulf of Maine's cooler water is buying us daytime bass while the rest of the coast fishes the dark — take advantage while it lasts.
body_markdown:
I took the outer route past Peaks and out toward Halfway Rock on Tuesday morning, and what struck me wasn't the fish so much as the water itself — that dark green-blue color holding steady, none of the murky freshwater push you sometimes get after a heavy rain week. Casco Bay is running clean and cool for late July, and that single fact is doing more work for us right now than any tide table.

Here's the thing worth understanding, and I say this having watched the coast from a professor's remove for thirty summers now: south of us, from Jersey up through Long Island Sound, the striper fishery has gone nocturnal. Surface temps down there are pushing into the mid-70s, forcing bass onto thermoclines and deep structure, feeding only at the edges of daylight or in full dark. We don't have that problem here. The Gulf of Maine keeps its foot on the brake, and Casco Bay's water — even inshore around the coves — hasn't hit that threshold. So our bass are still willing to work shallow ledges and estuary mouths in daylight, particularly on the push of the tide. That's a real advantage this time of year, and it's worth planning around rather than assuming it'll last forever.

Mackerel are the backbone of the week. Schools have been thick off Halfway Rock and along the drop north of Jewell Island, showing up as nervous water and diving terns any time from mid-morning through early afternoon. Small chrome Swedish Pimples and mackerel jigs strung three or four to a line, dropped to 20-30 feet and worked with a short snap, are filling coolers fast. If you're marking bait but not connecting, drop deeper — I've had mornings where the mackerel sat tight to bottom in 40 feet even with birds working the surface, chasing something smaller we couldn't see.

Those mackerel schools are exactly why the striper bite has held up on the ledges around Bailey Island and out toward Cape Small. Bass are shadowing the bait, and I've taken fish to 30 inches working live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, fished right on the last two hours of the incoming near the ledges off Ragged Island. The take is subtle — a slow pull-down rather than a hit — so keep your drag light and let the fish load up before you set. Bucktails in white and chartreuse, 1 to 1.5 ounce, worked slow along bottom on the slack before the ebb, have also been productive around the mouth of the New Meadows River and the ledges off Cundy's Harbor. Nothing explosive, but steady — three or four keeper-class fish on a good tide, which for mid-summer bay fishing is a fair result.

Groundfish remain a Halfway Rock story, as they generally are this time of year. Cod and a scattering of haddock are holding on the structure in 60 to 90 feet, and the pattern hasn't changed much from what I described last week — the slack water either side of the tide change is when you want your bait down. Clam and herring chunks on a standard cod rig, fished tight to the rock's northern face where the bottom breaks up into boulder and gravel, have produced fish in the 6 to 10 pound range. It's not fast fishing. You're putting in time for quality over quantity, and that's been true of this rock for as long as I've fished it. Two Lights hasn't been as productive for groundfish this month — too much boat traffic and not enough structure relief close in — but it remains a reliable spot for mackerel and the occasional bluefish push when the bait runs thick along that stretch of coast.

Bluefish have made a modest appearance in the bay's outer reaches, nothing like the blitz conditions unfolding to our south where blues are tearing through bunker schools from Jersey to western Long Island Sound. Here we're seeing occasional cutoffs on mackerel rigs and the odd blue mixed in with striper catches off Jewell and Cliff Island, nothing organized enough to target specifically yet. Worth keeping a wire leader in the tackle box regardless.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect steady action on the tide changes through this stable weather stretch — and that's held true. The bay hasn't given us anything dramatic, but it's given us dependable fishing, which this time of year is worth more than a hot week that burns out fast.

Looking ahead, the moon is working toward the next quarter, which means tidal swings will be moderate rather than extreme — good news for anyone fishing the ledges, since you won't be fighting the kind of hard current that makes bottom fishing at Halfway Rock miserable. If the weather holds calm through the weekend, I'd focus effort on the first two hours of the incoming at the Cape Small ledges for bass, and shift to Halfway Rock's slack water windows for cod and haddock. If a front comes through and stirs up the surface, expect the mackerel to push deeper and the bass bite to compress into narrower windows around first light. Either way, this cooler water is a gift right now — the rest of the coast would trade for it. Fish it while you've got it.
